entries.name: scaling hypothesis
entries.senseHere: The bet that general intelligence comes from simple artificial neurons and learning rules, run on enough data and computing power. The strong form needs no new inventions beyond a scalable design. The weak form says new algorithms are still needed piece by piece.

entries.name: GPT-3
entries.background: A very large language model released by OpenAI in 2020, with 175 billion adjustable numbers (parameters). It was trained to predict the next word of Internet text.

entries.name: meta-learning
entries.senseHere: A model's ability to pick up a new task from a few examples or a description given in the prompt, without retraining. GPT-3 showed this without being built for it.

entries.name: GPT-2
entries.background: OpenAI's 2019 language model with 1.5 billion parameters, known for generating fluent text. GPT-3 is its much larger successor.

entries.name: OpenAI
entries.background: The AI lab that built GPT-3. It began as a nonprofit and later added a for-profit arm to raise money for large computing bills.

entries.name: blessings of scale
entries.senseHere: The observation that making neural networks, data and computing bigger makes hard problems easier. Models become more stable, more general and better at learning new tasks.

entries.name: Transformer
entries.background: A neural network design from 2017 that uses attention to relate each word to the others. It underlies GPT and most modern language models.

entries.name: scaling laws
entries.senseHere: Smooth, predictable curves showing that a model's error falls steadily as model size, data and computing grow. They let the author forecast what bigger models could do.

entries.name: unsupervised learning
entries.background: Learning from raw data without human-written labels, such as text predicting its own next word. Supervised learning needs labeled examples.

entries.name: reinforcement learning
entries.background: Training a system by giving it rewards for good actions, as in game-playing AIs. The deep version uses large neural networks.

entries.name: ensemble
entries.senseHere: The view that a big network holds countless smaller networks inside it. Their errors average out, favoring simple solutions that still grow more complex as the data demands.

entries.name: Hans Moravec
entries.background: Robotics researcher who forecast in the 1990s, from computer-power trends, when machines would match animal and then human brains. His dates pointed to the 2020s for human-level systems.

entries.name: connectionism
entries.background: The older school of AI that tries to build intelligence from networks of simple artificial neurons, the ancestor of deep learning.

entries.name: AGI
entries.background: Artificial general intelligence: a machine that can learn and do the full range of intellectual tasks a human can.

entries.name: Jukebox
entries.background: An OpenAI model from 2020 that generates raw audio music, including singing voices.

entries.name: pretraining thesis
entries.senseHere: The argument that predicting the next piece of text well enough forces a model to learn logic, cause and effect, and facts about the world.

entries.name: Turing-NLG
entries.background: A Microsoft language model with 17 billion parameters, the largest before GPT-3.

entries.name: AlphaGo Zero
entries.background: DeepMind game-playing programs that learned Go and other games largely by playing themselves. They showed that scaling simple learning methods can beat human experts.

entries.name: cross-entropy loss
entries.background: A score of how badly a model predicts the next item, where lower is better. For text it can be measured in bits per character, meaning how many yes-or-no questions of surprise remain.

entries.name: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
entries.background: A 2020 OpenAI paper showing language model error falling smoothly as size, data and computing rise.

entries.name: The Bitter Lesson
entries.background: An essay by Richard Sutton arguing that in AI, general methods that use more computing power eventually beat clever hand-built approaches.

entries.name: DeepMind
entries.background: A London AI lab owned by Google, known for AlphaGo and other game-playing systems.

entries.name: agency
entries.senseHere: The ability to pursue goals by planning actions. The author says it is a matter of degree, not a yes-or-no property. A model that imitates human text can therefore act like an agent when prompted.

entries.name: hardware overhang
entries.senseHere: A situation where computers powerful enough for a breakthrough already exist, but researchers have not yet tried to use them that way.

entries.name: Ilya Sutskever
entries.background: Deep learning researcher and OpenAI co-founder who long argued that large neural networks with enough data and computing would work.

entries.name: intentional stance
entries.background: Philosopher Daniel Dennett's idea that we can explain a system by treating it as having goals and beliefs, even when it is not obviously a mind.

entries.name: variational principle
entries.senseHere: Explaining a system as if it were trying to minimize or maximize one simple quantity, like a river seeking the lowest path. This gives the right answer more easily than tracking every atom.

entries.name: SayCan
entries.background: A Google system from 2022 that lets a robot follow spoken instructions by using a language model to plan steps.

entries.name: Janus
entries.background: A pseudonymous writer on language models who views GPT as a simulator of the world, not an agent.

entries.name: Conway's Game of Life
entries.background: A grid of cells that live or die by simple neighbor rules. It produces moving patterns such as gliders and static blocks called still lifes.

entries.name: Turing machine
entries.background: A mathematical model of a computer that follows rules to mark symbols on an endless tape. The Busy Beaver is the program that runs longest before halting among programs of a given size.

entries.name: Occam's razor
entries.background: The principle that, among explanations that fit the facts, the simplest one is preferred.
